newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dlr loses steam by late Tokyo after sharp rises.
newsitem.headline: Dlr loses steam by late Tokyo after sharp rises.

text.p: 0650 GMT TRADED HIGH/LOW AS OF 0600 GMT

The dollar lost steam after earlier rising to 115.80 yen by late Tokyo on Thursday as the greenback's downside risk remained despite finance ministry official Eisuke Sakakibara's attempt to talk up the dollar.
Sakakibara tried to brush aside market concerns, saying that Japan's trade surplus will not be a major issue at the summit meeting of the Group of Seven (G7) nations in Denver.

"A drastic expansion of the surplus cannot happen," Sakakibara said. Asked what he thought about market participants focusing on Japan's surplus, he said: "I think the issue is being played up excessively. People should try to understand more clearly the position of the United States."
Many traders were caught off guard by his remarks as they had sold dollars heavily until Tuesday, betting on the dollar's slide because of U.S. worries over Japan's rising surplus.
"It was a disaster...as many traders were forced to cut their positions in the face of a slew of dollar-boosting comments by Sakakibara," said one European bank dealer.
Sakakibara, who spoke at a closed-door financial seminar, was quoted as saying by those who attended the seminar that Japan's interest rates are unlikely to rise any time soon.

The dollar's rise accelerated after remarks by Tomomitsu Oba, former vice finance minister for international affairs. He said: "I think Mr Sakakibara has a slightly stronger yen in mind than what I think about exchange rates." Oba said he himself thought a dollar/yen rate of 120 yen was an appropriate level.
"Many operators had to buy back dollars with reluctance. As a result they posted heavy losses for today," said a dealer.

The dollar fell back in late Tokyo on speculation that U.S. auto makers will demand a weaker dollar when they meet President Bill Clinton on June 27 and on remarks by Koichi Kato, secretary-general of Japan's ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP). Kato told Reuters that the yen would strengthen further if Japan's trade surplus were to increase.
Many dealers were puzzled by the wild swing in the dollar/yen following remarks by Japanese monetary authorities.
"Sakakibara's remarks are again making it difficult to test 110 yen immediately, but the downside risk is intact," said a U.S. bank dealer in Tokyo.

Some dealers said they now see that the Japanese authorities are most comfortable with a dollar/yen rate of around 115 yen, but also complained about the verbal intervention by Japanese monetary authorities.

Ryohei Muramatsu, manager of the treasury and foreign exchange department at Commerzbank in Tokyo, said: "Authorities should seek stable exchange rates, but instead, they have become the cause of the recent wild movements in the markets."
"The dollar tends to overshoot sometimes, and it will be impossible for them to trap the dollar/yen rate in a certain range," he added.

Singapore dealers said Sakakibara's comments had caused the dollar to surge, but the 116 yen level was likely to provide a cap for the time being. Japanese exporters also sold dollars after the greenback's rise to 115.80 yen.

A Japanese bank dealer in Singapore said the main impetus for the dollar's rise had come from Sakakibara's quoted remark that Japan was not yet ready to raise interest rates. "That's what caused the push up from 113 to 115. But I think the market could retrace back to 113 with just any news," he said. ---Singapore newsroom (65-8703080) ---Tatsuo Ito in Tokyo 81-3-3432-1396
